turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: I don't think that things have progressed far enough that it's really impacted in a fundamental way how many people you would need to build an app of the scale of Cash App, for example. I think what's changed for us is much different and it has nothing to do with AI, it's what we talked about earlier is moving from our GM structure to a functional structure. And in our GM structure, our incentives were always to think of engineering headcount as a commodity. (00:45:09): And so we would just add more engineers if we wanted to build more features and the classic mythical man person month trap or whatever it's called. And I think that moving to a functional structure completely changes that and you're like, "Well, we can leverage common platforms, common modules, we can bring in experts from across the company to advise us on how better to do this." (00:45:38): And so those kinds of things I think have made it much different and how we hire and we no longer see engineers as a commodity to just add 100 people to go and build the next product in Cash App. But on the AI side, we're very much looking for people that are embracing these tools and that are eager to try and learn from it. We're not looking for people who are amazing AI practitioners on the get-go. (00:46:14): I think we have those people and we're interested in those people if they ever want to work with us. But I'm much more keen on looking for that college grad who just really is eager to learn about these tools and open to it, or even the veteran who has embraced these tools and figured it out. And that's kind of where we're optimizing for who we look for rather than a specific set of skills.
turns.zh: 我认为事情还没有取得足够的进展，以至于它真正从根本上影响了你需要多少人来构建一个像 Cash App 这样规模的应用程序。我认为我们的变化是非常不同的，这与人工智能无关，我们之前谈到的是从我们的GM结构转向职能结构。在我们的总经理结构中，我们的激励措施始终是将工程人员视为一种商品。 (00:45:09)：因此，如果我们想要构建更多功能和经典神话般的人月陷阱或其他任何名称，我们只需添加更多工程师即可。我认为转向功能性结构完全改变了这一点，你会想，“好吧，我们可以利用通用平台、通用模块，我们可以聘请整个公司的专家来为我们提供建议，告诉我们如何更好地做到这一点。” (00:45:38)：所以我认为这些事情已经让我们的招聘方式变得非常不同，我们不再将工程师视为一种商品，只需添加 100 人就可以在 Cash App 中构建下一个产品。但在人工智能方面，我们非常寻找拥抱这些工具并渴望尝试并从中学习的人。我们并不是在寻找一开始就成为出色的人工智能从业者的人。 (00:46:14)：我认为我们拥有这些人，如果他们愿意与我们合作，我们会对他们感兴趣。但我更热衷于寻找那些真正渴望了解这些工具并对其持开放态度的大学毕业生，甚至是接受这些工具并弄清楚它的退伍军人。这就是我们针对我们寻找的人而不是一组特定技能进行优化的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So essentially the biggest change is just looking for people that are embracing AI, not being like, "No, I don't need this stuff. I'm an amazing engineer. I don't need to use Cursor or Goose or all these things."
turns.zh: 因此，本质上最大的变化就是寻找拥抱人工智能的人，而不是说“不，我不需要这些东西。我是一位了不起的工程师。我不需要使用 Cursor 或 Goose 或所有这些东西。”

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, a learning mindset is how I would put it. This is something that Jack our CEO talks about a lot is he wants us to be a learning first company. So everything we do, every experiment that we ship, what can we learn from it and did we feel that we gave it our best shot? And I think that that's more important to him than even sort of coming up with the right business answer every time.
turns.zh: 是的，我会这么说，学习心态。这是我们的首席执行官杰克经常谈论的事情，他希望我们成为一家学习第一的公司。那么我们所做的一切，我们进行的每一个实验，我们可以从中学到什么，我们是否觉得我们已经尽力了？我认为这对他来说比每次都能提出正确的商业答案更重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What about when you're interviewing? Are you encouraging engineers to use AI tools as they're doing exercises? How did that change over the past year or two?
turns.zh: 面试的时候怎么办？您是否鼓励工程师在练习时使用人工智能工具？在过去的一两年里，情况发生了怎样的变化？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, we're starting to do that now. So traditionally we would just use CoderPad or something like that to wipe boards or a problem or even program it in Pseudocode or near Pseudocode. But now we're looking at can you use Vibe code to build something? How comfortable are you with these tools or how are you thinking about evolving with them as well? (00:48:04): But it's early days yet I would say that it's not clear to me that necessarily how someone knows how to use, be it Goose or Cursor or any of these other tools matters that much to whether they're a good engineer. I still think that things that we interviewed for in the past, a critical mindset, the ability to really understand deeply the technical nature of a problem is still much more important than whether you're a fully AI native programmer or not.
turns.zh: 是的，我们现在就开始这样做。因此，传统上我们只会使用 CoderPad 或类似的东西来擦除电路板或问题，甚至用伪代码或接近伪代码对其进行编程。但现在我们正在考虑是否可以使用 Vibe 代码来构建某些东西？您对这些工具的使用程度如何，或者您如何考虑使用它们进行改进？ (00:48:04)：但现在还为时过早，我想说的是，我还不清楚一个人如何知道如何使用，无论是 Goose 还是 Cursor 或任何其他工具，对于他们是否是一名优秀的工程师来说都至关重要。我仍然认为我们过去面试的东西，批判性的心态，真正深入理解问题的技术本质的能力，仍然比你是否是一个完全的人工智能原生程序员重要得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another question that I've always been thinking about a lot of people wonder is what level of engineer is most benefiting from these tools? You could argue it's the junior engineers now, they could just get all this work done. You could argue it's senior engineers because they know so much more about how things work and now they could just orchestrate thousands of agents doing their bidding. What have you seen in terms of which level is benefiting most?
turns.zh: 我一直在思考很多人想知道的另一个问题是，什么级别的工程师最能从这些工具中受益？你可能会说现在是初级工程师，他们可以完成所有这些工作。你可能会说这是高级工程师，因为他们对事物的工作原理了解得更多，现在他们可以安排数千名代理执行他们的命令。您认为哪个级别受益最大？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, so two answers to that. One is you're definitely right that the more senior and the more junior they are, the more comfortable or the more eager they are to adopt these AI tools. And I think that's for a variety of reasons, including some of them that you named. I think the senior people really understand in great depth how everything works. (00:49:18): And so they're almost relieved that this tool exists that can go and do all these things that they've done a million times before and couldn't be bothered. And then the junior people are like my niece and nephew on a BlackBerry or something, they're just blitzing through things, not BlackBerry in the early days and iPhones now, they're blitzing through a text message when I'm still seek and destroying through my keyboard, shows you how old I am. (00:49:50): So I think there's that, but I think the non-technical people using AI agents and programming tools to build things is really what's been surprising and really amazing. And I think that speaks to how these roles are going to evolve in the future. The lines are going to be blurred between whether you're in legal or in risk or in engineering and design even. And so I think that the people that are able to embrace it to optimize for their particular work day and their particular set of tasks are really who are showing the most impact from these tools.
turns.zh: 是的，所以有两个答案。一是你绝对是对的，他们越高级和越初级，他们就越舒服或更渴望采用这些人工智能工具。我认为这是出于多种原因，包括您提到的一些原因。我认为资深人士确实非常深入地了解一切是如何运作的。 (00:49:18)：所以他们几乎松了口气，因为这个工具的存在可以完成所有这些他们以前已经做过一百万次而不会被打扰的事情。然后初级人员就像我的侄女和侄子一样使用黑莓或其他东西，他们只是快速浏览东西，而不是早期的黑莓和现在的iPhone，当我还在寻找时他们快速浏览短信并通过键盘破坏，告诉你我有多大。 (00:49:50)：所以我认为是这样的，但我认为非技术人员使用人工智能代理和编程工具来构建东西确实是令人惊讶和令人惊奇的。我认为这说明了这些角色未来将如何演变。无论您处于法律还是风险之中，甚至在工程和设计方面，界限都将变得模糊。因此，我认为那些能够利用它来优化他们的特定工作日和特定任务集的人确实是从这些工具中表现出最大影响的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting. No one talks about that element of engineering productivity, which is the reduction of asks from all the other parts of the company to build random one-off things. That feels like a huge productivity gain for engineers.
turns.zh: 这很有趣。没有人谈论工程生产力的这一要素，即减少公司所有其他部门构建随机一次性产品的要求。对于工程师来说，这感觉像是巨大的生产力提升。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: It is massive, although I think that it's a little bit like the analogy of if you build a bigger highway, you'll just get more cars on the road. So I think the fact that everyone's building software means that there's more software to be built, more coordination to happen, and everyone's more eager to ship things faster and with greater results. And so we're just seeing an overall uptake in velocity and the ask for more features, if that makes sense. Yeah.
turns.zh: 它很大，尽管我认为这有点像如果你建造一条更大的高速公路，你就会在路上看到更多的汽车。因此，我认为每个人都在构建软件这一事实意味着有更多的软件需要构建，需要进行更多的协调，并且每个人都更渴望更快地交付产品并取得更好的成果。因此，我们只是看到速度的整体提升以及对更多功能的需求（如果这有意义的话）。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. And it connects to your point about you're not slowing hiring. What I'm hearing is just headcount, hiring desires for more engineers, more product people is not slowing at all. You're basically, it's as if AI wasn't really there.
turns.zh: 绝对地。这与你关于你没有放慢招聘的观点有关。我听到的只是员工人数，招聘更多工程师、更多产品人员的愿望丝毫没有放缓。基本上，就好像人工智能并不真正存在一样。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: We're being more thoughtful about it. So like I said, we were looking at as a commodity in the GM era, and now that we're functional, it's much less about how many engineers we need as a function of the number of features we have in Square or Cash App and in the functional org structure, we think of it much more as what are the areas of optimization? Where can we build depth and what really accelerates our priorities through things like modularization reuse and going deep into platforms.
turns.zh: 我们对此更加深思熟虑。所以就像我说的，我们在通用汽车时代将其视为一种商品，现在我们已经发挥了作用，我们需要多少工程师就不再是我们需要多少工程师的问题，而是我们在 Square 或 Cash App 以及功能组织结构中拥有的功能数量的函数，我们更多地将其视为优化的领域是什么？我们可以在哪里构建深度，以及通过模块化重用和深入平台等真正加速我们的优先事项。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this hot take of if you're trying to be more productive, forget AI, just re-org into a functional structure.
turns.zh: 如果你想提高生产力，忘记人工智能，只需重新组织成一个功能结构，我喜欢这个热门观点。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: It's not wrong in some ways. So here's another really interesting example where we are trying to improve our build times and you were using Goose and a lot of other tools to help us with this too, and they've done remarkable things. So we have this really cool tool that analyzes our test suites and selects the right test to run for changes that were made. (00:52:50): So we cut down basically 50% of test runs this way, which is pretty great, and we're not warming the planet as much with all these unnecessary CPU cycles being wasted on tests. But then things like offloading tests to the cloud or simply just deleting tests that don't make sense anymore, probably save you two to three times that. (00:53:14): So there is still a portfolio approach that you need to take for lack of a better term. It's like that example I told you earlier about should we buy a vendor tool? Should we build this in-house? It's like, "Well, do we even need to do this process at all?" So in some ways, structure matters more than the efficacy of the tools you have.
turns.zh: 从某些方面来说这并没有错。这是另一个非常有趣的例子，我们正在尝试缩短构建时间，而您也使用 Goose 和许多其他工具来帮助我们完成此任务，他们已经做了一些了不起的事情。因此，我们拥有这个非常酷的工具，可以分析我们的测试套件并选择正确的测试来运行所做的更改。 (00:52:50)：所以我们通过这种方式基本上减少了 50% 的测试运行，这非常好，而且我们不会因为所有这些不必要的 CPU 周期浪费在测试上而导致地球变暖。但是，像将测试卸载到云端或只是删除不再有意义的测试之类的事情可能会为您节省两到三倍的时间。 (00:53:14)：因此，由于缺乏更好的术语，您仍然需要采取投资组合方法。就像我之前告诉过你的那个例子，我们应该购买供应商工具吗？我们应该在内部构建这个吗？就像，“好吧，我们是否需要执行这个过程？”因此，在某些方面，结构比所拥有工具的功效更重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wise words makes me think about Elon has this whole process for optimize stuff and one of the steps is like, "Do we even need this thing before we start out optimizing and automating it?" Before I zoom out and ask about just general lessons that you've learned over the course of your career, is there anything else that you think might be really valuable or useful to folks that are trying to lean in further into AI or just help their teams think a little bit more forward thinking?
turns.zh: 明智的话让我想到埃隆有整个优化过程，其中一个步骤就像是，“在我们开始优化和自动化之前，我们是否需要这个东西？”在我缩小范围并询问您在职业生涯中学到的一般经验之前，您认为对于那些试图进一步深入人工智能或只是帮助他们的团队思考更多前瞻性思维的人来说，还有什么可能真正有价值或有用的东西吗？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: I would say really try and use these tools yourself. So the way in which I think we've been able to drive most of the adoption is Jack uses Goose, I use Goose, our executive team all have used Goose and use it regularly and use other AI programming tools and assistance as well, and we do it every single day. (00:54:31): And so we learn a lot about how our own workflow can change, and that's going to tell you so much more about how are you going to change your organization's workflow than if you're reading a bunch of think pieces on LinkedIn or Harvard Business Review or whatever it is, and then trying to get your teams to follow suit. So I think we do this with everything. It's feel it, use the product yourself, feel it, understand its strengths and weaknesses and its ergonomics, and then figure out how to apply it to your teams.
turns.zh: 我想说的是，请亲自尝试并使用这些工具。因此，我认为我们能够推动大部分采用的方式是 Jack 使用 Goose，我使用 Goose，我们的执行团队都使用 Goose 并定期使用它，还使用其他人工智能编程工具和帮助，我们每天都这样做。 (00:54:31)：因此，我们了解了很多关于我们自己的工作流程如何改变的知识，这将告诉你更多关于如何改变组织工作流程的信息，而不是你在 LinkedIn 或哈佛商业评论或其他任何网站上阅读一堆思考文章，然后试图让你的团队效仿。所以我认为我们在所有事情上都这样做。就是感受它，亲自使用产品，感受它，了解它的优点和缺点以及它的人体工程学原理，然后弄清楚如何将它应用到你的团队中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something I've found helpful in doing that, which I completely agree with, which is stop reading about it, stop listening to us talking about it, just build some stuff. The thing that I found really helpful there is have a specific task or problem you want to solve for yourself because that really motivates you and makes it very real. (00:55:21): For example, just the other day, I was trying to pull images out of a Google Doc. Google Doc, it's like I think of it as Hotel California. You put images in there, but there's no way to get them back out unless you do some crazy stuff. So I just went to Lovable and like Bill an app, or I can give you a Google Doc URL and let me download the images real easily and bam. Perfect.
turns.zh: 我发现这样做很有帮助，我完全同意，那就是停止阅读它，停止听我们谈论它，只是构建一些东西。我发现真正有帮助的是有一个你想要自己解决的特定任务或问题，因为这确实会激励你并使之变得非常现实。 (00:55:21)：例如，就在前几天，我试图从 Google 文档中提取图像。谷歌文档，我把它想象成《加州旅馆》。你把图像放在那里，但除非你做一些疯狂的事情，否则没有办法把它们取出来。所以我就去了 Lovable 并给 Bill 点了一个应用程序，或者我可以给你一个 Google 文档 URL，让我轻松下载图像，然后就可以了。完美的。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, great example. I did something like this a couple months ago as well, where my son has a whole bunch of therapies, he has additional needs, and so I was trying to gather the receipts for all these therapies and share them with my wife and she will claim it from our insurer, and I was really struggling to do this because they're in various forms. (00:56:05): There are screenshots in some cases or PDFs or whatever. So I asked Goose to do this and it was all sitting on my laptop and Goose figured out that it could put all of these receipts into my Apple Notes app into a single note. It converted it to HTML so it would sync seamlessly to my phone and then I could email it or share it with her from there. (00:56:30): And that's just something I just never would've thought of. And it did this using Apple Script, so it just controlled my computer for me in the background. Yeah, so these are surprising ways in which these tools help us, and the more you use them to solve real problems to your point, the more you understand what their strengths are and where you can deploy them.
turns.zh: 是的，很好的例子。几个月前我也做了类似的事情，我的儿子接受了一大堆治疗，他有额外的需求，所以我试图收集所有这些治疗的收据并与我的妻子分享，她将从我们的保险公司索赔，我真的很难做到这一点，因为它们有多种形式。 (00:56:05)：在某些情况下有屏幕截图或 PDF 等。因此，我要求 Goose 这样做，所有这些都放在我的笔记本电脑上，Goose 发现它可以将所有这些收据放入我的 Apple Notes 应用程序中，形成一个笔记。它将其转换为 HTML，以便它可以无缝同步到我的手机，然后我可以通过电子邮件发送或从那里与她分享。 (00:56:30)：这是我从未想到过的事情。它使用 Apple Script 来完成此操作，因此它只是在后台为我控制我的计算机。是的，这些工具以令人惊讶的方式帮助我们，你越多地使用它们来解决你的观点的实际问题，你就越了解它们的优势是什么以及可以在哪里部署它们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this example. So did you just go to Goose and be like, "Here's the problem I have, how would you solve it?"
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个例子。那么你是否只是去找 Goose 并说：“这是我遇到的问题，你会如何解决它？”

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, pretty much. I said, "I have all these receipts there in Google Drive, so we have similar origin problem there and I need to get them into a single form and I need to collate the totals and do all this." So it tried a few approaches first. It tried to download them and it tried to read them using a PDF reader and this and that. And then the thing about Goose that I think a lot of the other AI agents learn from us as well is if it tries a few things and fails, it'll back up and it'll try a different route and it'll just keep going until it makes some progress. (00:57:33): And that's what it did. Then it picked Apple Script as a way to do it because it had the MCP extension to control my computer, and this is the same thing that our engineer, we were talking about the other day uses to watch his screen and things like that, but this was a very focused problem and it managed to do that. So yeah, it's surprising what these tools can do and allowing them the flexibility to do that is a big part of learning how to use them.
turns.zh: 是的，差不多。我说：“我在 Google 云端硬盘上有所有这些收据，所以我们那里有类似的来源问题，我需要将它们放入一个表格中，我需要整理总数并完成所有这些工作。”因此它首先尝试了几种方法。它尝试下载它们并尝试使用 PDF 阅读器阅读它们等等。然后，我认为许多其他人工智能代理也向我们学习了关于 Goose 的事情，如果它尝试了一些事情并且失败了，它会备份并尝试不同的路线，并且它会继续前进，直到取得一些进展。 (00:57:33)：这就是它所做的。然后它选择了 Apple Script 作为实现这一目标的方法，因为它有 MCP 扩展来控制我的计算机，这与我们的工程师，我们前几天谈论的用来观看他的屏幕和类似的东西是一样的，但这是一个非常集中的问题，它成功地做到了这一点。所以，是的，这些工具的功能令人惊讶，让它们能够灵活地执行这些操作是学习如何使用它们的一个重要部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's cool. I love the, by the way, can you run Goose as a regular person? Can you just download Goose and use that instead of Claude?
turns.zh: 这很酷。我喜欢这个，顺便问一下，你能像普通人一样经营 Goose 吗？您可以直接下载 Goose 并使用它来代替 Claude 吗？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. Yeah. You can just download it from our URL. We can share it in the show notes for you and yeah, you can install it. It comes for Mac and Windows and Linux I believe. It's an electron app, so it'll work on all of them. It also has a command line, so for people who are more comfortable using that, we have that UI as well.
turns.zh: 是的，绝对是。是的。您只需从我们的 URL 下载即可。我们可以在演出笔记中为您分享它，是的，您可以安装它。我相信它适用于 Mac、Windows 和 Linux。这是一个电子应用程序，因此它适用于所有这些应用程序。它还有一个命令行，因此对于更习惯使用命令行的人来说，我们也有该用户界面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, you really are competing with these massive foundational model companies building. What's the simplest way to compare Goose to something else? Is it like this Claude code, this simplest comparison or something else?
turns.zh: 哇，你真的在​​与这些大规模的基础模型公司竞争。将 Goose 与其他产品进行比较的最简单方法是什么？是像这个克劳德代码，这个最简单的比较还是别的什么？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: I think it's a bit different than Claude Code because at its core, Goose is a platform that implements MCPs. So MCPs give it this dynamically extensible nature so it can do all of these things for you, whether it's automating things like we were talking about with Google Docs and notes and things like that, or it can do straight up programming tasks for you using other MCPs. (00:59:11): It can index code and do it that way. So it's really more of an extensible platform. So I would say it sits somewhere between your classic AI assistant where you just ask it, "What's the weather today? Can you calculate how many months it's been since this date?" Or whatever it is, to the more focused cursors and Claude codes of the world.
turns.zh: 我认为它与 Claude Code 有点不同，因为从本质上讲，Goose 是一个实现 MCP 的平台。因此，MCP 赋予它动态可扩展的特性，因此它可以为您完成所有这些事情，无论是像我们讨论的 Google 文档和注释之类的自动化事情，还是可以使用其他 MCP 为您直接完成编程任务。 (00:59:11)：它可以索引代码并以这种方式执行。所以它实际上更像是一个可扩展的平台。所以我想说它介于经典的人工智能助手之间，你只需问它，“今天天气怎么样？你能计算出从这个日期到现在已经有多少个月了吗？”或者无论它是什么，对于世界上更集中的光标和克劳德代码。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Basically, it's everything combined wholly and free. You pay for the LM tokens, but yeah.
turns.zh: 基本上，一切都是完全免费的。你需要支付 LM 代币的费用，但是是的。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, there's not like an open source models which-
turns.zh: 是的，没有像开源模型那样-

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God, this is crazy. What a cool team to be on building Goose at Block. Must having must be having so much fun. Oh man. Okay. Let me zoom out a little bit. So you've been CTO in LinkedIn right now for just about two years. What's something that you wish you knew before you stepped in this role? If you could go back a couple years and just whisper a few tips and tricks or lessons into your ear, what would they be?
turns.zh: 天哪，这太疯狂了。在 Block 上构建 Goose 的团队真是太酷了。一定有很多乐趣。噢，伙计。好的。让我把镜头缩小一点。您现在在 LinkedIn 担任 CTO 大约两年了。在担任这个角色之前，您希望了解什么？如果你可以回到几年前，在你耳边低声说出一些技巧、窍门或教训，它们会是什么？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: I think maybe two different things. One is just the power of Conway's Law, like we talked about before. It's like how difficult it is to change outcomes without changing the structure of relationships between people in an organization. And I think I always kind of knew that at some level, but really appreciating it in a visceral way is big. The other thing that I really learned the hard way maybe is you only hear about it when things are going wrong. (01:00:49): So when things are going well, you kind of have this eerie silence and you're like, "Well, am I doing the right things here? Am I focusing on the right problems?" So having a bit of judgment, having a bit of time to step back and look at things holistically, those are things that you really need to make time for and do on a regular basis, which I wish I had known when I took up the role.
turns.zh: 我想也许是两种不同的事情。一是康威定律的力量，就像我们之前谈到的那样。这就像在不改变组织中人与人之间的关系结构的情况下改变结果是多么困难。我想我在某种程度上总是知道这一点，但真正发自内心地欣赏它是很重要的。我真正学到的另一件事是，也许只有当事情出错时你才会听到它。 (01:00:49)：所以当事情进展顺利时，你会感到一种令人毛骨悚然的沉默，你会想，“好吧，我在这里做的事情正确吗？我关注的问题正确吗？”因此，有一点判断力，有一点时间退后一步，从整体上看待事情，这些都是你真正需要腾出时间并定期做的事情，我希望在我担任这个角色时就知道这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Looking back at your time at Block, I keep trying to, I almost say Square because I'm so used to that over the air, but I know Block is the name of the broader company and Square is just one. Just so people understand, Square is one business unit, one product within Block.
turns.zh: 回顾你在 Block 的时光，我一直在努力，我几乎会说 Square，因为我已经习惯了在广播中这样说，但我知道 Block 是更广泛的公司的名称，而 Square 只是其中之一。正如人们所理解的，Square 是 Block 中的一个业务部门、一种产品。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Correct, yeah, we have Square, Afterpay, Cash App and TIDAL are four major brands, and then we also have Bitkey and Proto that are focused on Bitcoin for us and we chip hardware in those two brands.
turns.zh: 是的，我们有 Square、Afterpay、Cash App 和 TIDAL 四个主要品牌，然后我们还有 Bitkey 和 Proto，它们专注于比特币，我们在这两个品牌中使用芯片硬件。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. I think that some people are like, what are you guys talking about? Okay, cool. So reflecting back on your time at Block, what's maybe the most counterintuitive lesson you've learned about building products or building teams that goes against what most people believe, say common startup wisdom?
turns.zh: 好的，太好了。我想有些人会问，你们在说什么？好吧，酷。因此，回想一下您在 Block 的时光，您在构建产品或构建团队时学到的最违反直觉的教训可能是什么，这些教训与大多数人的看法（即常见的创业智慧）背道而驰？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: I think code quality is one. Being an engineer. I learned this very early on and it keeps coming true over and over and over again. A lot of engineers think that code quality is important to building a successful product. The two have nothing to do with each other, but my favorite example is YouTube. I was working at Google around the time YouTube was acquired and I just remember there was this whole wash of angst about how horrible the YouTube code base is and how terrible their architecture is, and they're storing videos as blobs in MySQL and whatnot. (01:02:41): And you could argue that YouTube is the most successful product at Google by a long way, maybe more successful than many of their others combined. And so it really has very little to do with how well it was architected because the flip side of that Google video, which is product that I don't know if people remember, it existed before YouTube. It supported more formats, it supported higher resolution. (01:03:11): You could upload hour long videos, YouTube had none of this. It just had the one or two minute quick video thing and it's far and away, blown away its competition. And so I think just keeping that front and center is why are we building these tools or these apps or these products? They're for people to solve a specific problem. So in our case, it's for a square merchant to make a sale, to sell coffee to you or to sell something they've made. And that's really what's important. (01:03:49): It's not really important how well our Android platform performs unless it's serving that need. And so I think that's been a really hard one for me over my career. And I continually encounter engineers who think we need to refactor, we need to do this in a better way. And then I'm like, "No, all this code could be thrown away tomorrow. So just focus on what we're trying to build and whom we're trying to build for."
turns.zh: 我认为代码质量是其中之一。作为一名工程师。我很早就知道了这一点，而且它一次又一次地成为现实。许多工程师认为代码质量对于构建成功的产品非常重要。这两者没有任何关系，但我最喜欢的例子是 YouTube。 YouTube 被收购的时候，我正在 Google 工作，我只记得 YouTube 代码库是多么糟糕，他们的架构是多么糟糕，而且他们将视频作为 blob 存储在 MySQL 之类的东西中，人们对此充满了焦虑。 (01:02:41)：你可以说 YouTube 是 Google 迄今为止最成功的产品，也许比其他许多产品的总和还要成功。所以它实际上与它的架构有多好没有什么关系，因为谷歌视频的另一面，我不知道人们是否还记得，它是在 YouTube 之前就存在的产品。它支持更多格式，支持更高的分辨率。 (01:03:11)：您可以上传长达一小时的视频，而 YouTube 没有这些。它只有一两分钟的快速视频，而且距离很远，远远超过了它的竞争对手。因此，我认为保持这一点就是我们构建这些工具、这些应用程序或这些产品的原因？它们是为了人们解决特定问题。因此，在我们的例子中，这是一个方形商人进行销售，向您出售咖啡或出售他们制作的东西。这才是真正重要的。 (01:03:49)：除非我们的 Android 平台能够满足这一需求，否则它的性能如何并不重要。所以我认为这对我的职业生涯来说是非常艰难的。我不断遇到认为我们需要重构的工程师，我们需要以更好的方式做到这一点。然后我想，“不，所有这些代码明天都可能被扔掉。所以只需关注我们正在尝试构建的内容以及我们正在尝试为谁构建。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is an incredible insight and lesson. This YouTube story is so fun and such a good example. You're saying they were storing the video content in a MySQL set like row and column as a blob data.
turns.zh: 这是令人难以置信的见解和教训。 YouTube 上的这个故事非常有趣，也是一个很好的例子。你是说他们将视频内容存储在 MySQL 集合中，如行和列作为 blob 数据。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, this is what, I didn't actually look the code so I couldn't verify it, but this was the common wisdom. And then they had an entirely Python stack that was incredibly slow compared to the state-of-the-art C++ and Java servers that we had hyper-optimized at Google back in those days.
turns.zh: 是的，就是这样，我实际上没有查看代码，所以无法验证它，但这是常识。然后他们有一个完全 Python 堆栈，与当时我们在 Google 进行超优化的最先进的 C++ 和 Java 服务器相比，速度慢得令人难以置信。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is hilarious. It makes me think about also companies when you look inside a company, if you work at a company, you're just like, "This is just pure chaos. No one knows what's going on. This is just about to all fall apart." And that's basically what it's like at every successful hyper-growth company.
turns.zh: 太搞笑了。这让我想到了公司，当你观察一家公司的内部时，如果你在一家公司工作，你就会想，“这纯粹是混乱。没有人知道发生了什么。这一切都快要崩溃了。”这基本上就是每家成功的高速增长公司的情况。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, there's some truth to that for sure. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，这确实有一定道理。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so I think again, it's just there's so much more that is more important to the success of a business. And it's what you said is are you solving a real problem for people? Can you get in their hands? Can you continue solving real problems for them? It's not about the quality of the code, it's not how well you operate internally.
turns.zh: 所以我再次认为，对于企业的成功来说，还有更多更重要的事情。你说的是你在为人们解决真正的问题吗？你能到他们手里吗？你能继续为他们解决实际问题吗？这与代码的质量无关，与内部运作的情况无关。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Absolutely. I think on Cash App we had that as well. So in the early days of Cash App, I was head of engineering from when we were about 10 engineers to 200 plus and took us to about 10 plus or 20 million users thereabouts. And there was a very similar thing there. From the outside it looked like everything was really chaotic. It's like people would build random experiments and ship them and it just didn't look like we were following strict policies on things like software life cycle and stuff like that, and it was kind of true. (01:06:13): And my philosophy was always, we have all these brilliant engineers and I'm going to do more harm than good by trying to harness them into very strict blinkered areas. If they want to spin their wheels building something that is a complete waste of time for a little bit. But at the same time, if they're delivering these amazing things on the flip side, then I'll almost allow that. I'll be okay with that. (01:06:44): And it's a fine balance because engineers can really go off and into rabbit holes if you let them. But yeah, there's a certain amount of creativity that chaos breeds and you have to know how to build controlled chaos in some ways. So you have to create a foundation that isn't liable to rupture. You have major liability problems or something like that, or you're going to lose money in our case. And so as long as those things are bedded down and you allow your engineers to have the freedom to experiment and iterate and do the things that energizes them, that's the ideal.
turns.zh: 绝对地。我想在 Cash App 上我们也有这样的功能。因此，在 Cash App 的早期，我担任工程主管，当时我们有大约 10 名工程师，现在有 200 多名工程师，并带领我们拥有了大约 10 多名或 2000 万左右的用户。那里有一个非常相似的事情。从外面看来，一切真的很混乱。就像人们会随机进行实验并交付它们，但看起来我们并没有在软件生命周期之类的事情上遵循严格的政策，这确实是事实。 (01:06:13)：我的理念始终是，我们拥有所有这些才华横溢的工程师，而我试图将他们纳入非常严格的狭隘领域，弊大于利。如果他们想继续开发一些东西，那完全是浪费时间。但与此同时，如果他们在另一方面提供了这些令人惊奇的东西，那么我几乎会允许这样做。我会同意的。 (01:06:44)：这是一个很好的平衡，因为如果你允许的话，工程师真的可以进入兔子洞。但是，是的，混乱会产生一定的创造力，你必须知道如何以某种方式构建受控的混乱。因此，您必须创建一个不易破裂的基础。你有重大的责任问题或类似的问题，否则你就会在我们的案例中赔钱。因此，只要这些事情都落实下来，并且允许工程师自由地进行实验和迭代，并做那些激发他们活力的事情，那就是理想的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of controlled chaos, one of your titles during your time at Block, I guess this was while you were actually at Square, was Mad Scientist for four and a half years.
turns.zh: 说到受控混乱，你在 Block 工作期间的作品之一（我猜这是你在 Square 工作的时候）是《疯狂科学家》（Mad Scientist）四年半了。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, that was a time when I was working part-time, mostly because I had very young kids with lots of additional needs and I was a consultant on various different projects and I was trying to help some wacky things get off the ground. And yeah, I'm really grateful to Block that they afforded me the freedom to have that role in my career as well.
turns.zh: 是的，那是我兼职工作的时候，主要是因为我有非常年幼的孩子，他们有很多额外的需求，而我是各种不同项目的顾问，我试图帮助一些古怪的事情取得进展。是的，我真的很感谢布洛克，他们给了我在职业生涯中扮演这个角色的自由。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe one more question before I take us to Fail Corner, which I'll explain. So you've shared a few lessons of things you've learned over the course of your career. Are there any other, just let's say core leadership lessons that you've learned that you think have been important to you being successful at the work that you've done?
turns.zh: 在带我们去“失败角”之前也许还有一个问题，我将对此进行解释。您分享了您在职业生涯中学到的一些经验教训。还有其他你学到的、你认为对你在工作中取得成功很重要的核心领导力课程吗？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: I think start small with everything. If you try to boil the ocean to make a cup of tea, I don't know who said that, but it's a really a useful phrase that I keep coming back to. You'll never get there. So if you're making a cup of tea, just make the cup of tea. You don't need to boil all the water that there is.
turns.zh: 我认为凡事都要从小事做起。如果你试图把海洋煮沸来泡一杯茶，我不知道这句话是谁说的，但这是一个非常有用的短语，我不断地想起。你永远也到不了那里。所以，如果你要泡一杯茶，就泡一杯茶吧。您不需要将所有的水都煮沸。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That sounds like really not delicious tea. Ocean water.
turns.zh: 听起来确实不是什么好茶。海水。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, I think there's another one of, I think Carl Sagan said, "If you want to make an apple pie from scratch, you have to first invent the universe." So it's like narrow your scope to the thing that's in front of you and that's achievable. And so that I think is really important and that's one of our core tenets and always has been even when we were just Square in the early days, start small.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为还有另一个，我认为卡尔·萨根说过，“如果你想从头开始制作苹果派，你必须首先发明宇宙。”所以这就像将你的范围缩小到你面前的、可以实现的事情上。所以我认为这非常重要，这是我们的核心原则之一，即使在我们早期只是 Square 的时候，也是如此，从小事做起。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example that maybe worked really well or maybe didn't work?
turns.zh: 有没有一个可能工作得很好或者可能不起作用的例子？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, Goose started small. It was just an engineer working on their own time trying to build something that was useful and that satisfied a thesis that they had. So Brad, our creator of Goose, believed very early on, I think long before we heard the buzzword going around that agents would be how we unlock value from LLMs. And he built a proof concept and he shared it with a bunch of people. He shared it with Databricks and Anthropic, got them excited and learned a lot from them. (01:09:59): And so it just sort of built momentum from there. And even internally, it was quite a similar thing. Cash App itself was like that and Cash App started more or less as a hack week sort of idea and grew into a bigger and bigger and bigger thing. So a lot of our projects start with these small experiments that we try to then build on top of. We became the very first company that was a public company to launch a Bitcoin product. And that was again a hack week idea that actually Jack and me and another engineer worked on.
turns.zh: 是的，Goose 从小做起。这只是一名工程师在自己的时间里努力构建一些有用的东西并且满足他们的论文。因此，我们 Goose 的创造者 Brad 很早就相信，我认为早在我们听到“代理人”这个流行词之前，我们就可以从法学硕士中释放价值。他建立了一个证明概念，并与一群人分享。他与 Databricks 和 Anthropic 分享了这些内容，让他们兴奋不已，并从他们身上学到了很多东西。 (01:09:59)：所以它只是从那里建立了动力。即使在内部，情况也非常相似。 Cash App 本身就是这样，Cash App 一开始或多或少是作为黑客周的想法，后来发展成为一个越来越大的东西。因此，我们的许多项目都是从这些小实验开始的，然后我们尝试在此基础上进行构建。我们成为第一家推出比特币产品的上市公司。这又是一个黑客周的想法，实际上杰克和我以及另一位工程师正在研究这个想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was the hackathon team? You and Jack Dorsey and an engineer?
turns.zh: 那是黑客马拉松团队？你和杰克·多尔西还有一名工程师？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, it was the three of us.
turns.zh: 是的，就是我们三个人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Unreal.
turns.zh: 虚幻。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, and it was great. We went and bought a cup of coffee, a blue bottle, and it was bought using Bitcoin over cash card. And I'll tell you those in hindsight, probably the most expensive cup of coffee.
turns.zh: 是的，那真是太棒了。我们去买了一杯咖啡、一瓶蓝瓶咖啡，是用比特币通过现金卡购买的。事后我会告诉你，这可能是最昂贵的一杯咖啡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What was Bitcoin at? 20,000?
turns.zh: 比特币当时处于什么水平？ 20,000？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: I think it was 6,000 or 7,000 back then. I don't know.
turns.zh: 我想当时是六千或七千。我不知道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's like 120,000 now. Great.
turns.zh: 现在好像有12万了。伟大的。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: But yeah, it's an example of how you get to a working useful product to people if you focus on a small thing first in a build.
turns.zh: 但是，是的，这是一个例子，说明如果您首先关注构建中的小事情，那么您如何获得对人们有用的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And just to double down on this counter too. "Okay, we have a big idea, we're just going to put a bunch of resources on it and go big immediately."
turns.zh: 也只是为了在这个柜台上加倍努力。 “好吧，我们有一个伟大的想法，我们将投入大量资源并立即将其付诸实施。”

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. And I've been part of teams like that too. So in my career, I worked at Google on this product called Google Wave, which was trying to be everything to everyone and we were 70, 80 engineers building this thing before it even really had any users outside Google. And so I think that's an example of something that started big, tried to go big on day one and probably lacked some of that meeting the earth where reality lies and adapting accordingly.
turns.zh: 是的，绝对是。我也曾是这样的团队的一员。因此，在我的职业生涯中，我在 Google 开发了这款名为 Google Wave 的产品，该产品试图成为每个人的一切，我们有 70、80 名工程师在构建这个产品，甚至在它真正拥有 Google 之外的任何用户之前。所以我认为这是一个例子，它开始很大，在第一天就试图做大，但可能缺乏一些与现实所在的地球相结合并相应地适应的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I remember Google Wave. Absolutely. It was beautiful. A lot of hype. I don't remember what it was for specifically, but it looked really nice.
turns.zh: 我记得谷歌Wave。绝对地。很漂亮。很多炒作。我不记得它具体是做什么的，但它看起来非常好。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, a lot of learnings from that one for me. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，我从那件事中学到了很多东西。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What else? Any other big lessons?
turns.zh: 还有什么？还有其他重大教训吗？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Those two are the big ones, but I would also say question base assumptions on everything. Sometimes we get into traps where we are as professionals, hyper focused on what we're building that day, that week, that month. And we don't stop to think should we even build this at all? Or what's the purpose of building this? (01:12:46): Could we build something completely different that would matter more to our core reason for being? So I would say, yeah, question the sort of base assumptions. It's somewhat of a cliche, but you really need to remind yourself to apply it over and over and over again.
turns.zh: 这两个是最重要的，但我也会说对一切的假设都存在疑问。有时，我们会陷入陷阱，因为我们是专业人士，过度专注于那天、那周、那个月我们正在构建的东西。我们根本不会停下来思考我们是否应该建造这个？或者说建造这个的目的是什么？ (01:12:46)：我们能否构建一些完全不同的东西，对我们存在的核心理由更重要？所以我想说，是的，质疑这种基本假设。这有点陈词滥调，但你确实需要提醒自己一遍又一遍地应用它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I had a colleague of yours on the podcast back in the day, IO, who worked with you on Cash App.
turns.zh: 我当时在播客上有一位同事 IO，他在 Cash App 上与您一起工作。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He's a friend of mine, he's amazing. He had a quote along those lines of just like, I forget exactly what it was, but it was just get to the bare metal of the thing that you're working on, just touch the thing that you're building and go to the base of it to really understand what's going on. And I imagine that was really important with Building Cash App and Cash Card.
turns.zh: 他是我的朋友，他很棒。他引用了一句话，就像，我忘记了它到底是什么，但它只是触及你正在开发的东西的裸露金属，只需触摸你正在构建的东西并深入到它的底部，以真正了解正在发生的事情。我认为这对于构建现金应用程序和现金卡非常重要。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, IO is one of the best product people I've ever worked with and one of my closest friends actually. So absolutely with him, and you on that one, yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，IO 是我合作过的最好的产品人员之一，实际上也是我最亲密的朋友之一。所以绝对和他在一起，还有你，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I'm going to take us to a recurring segment on the podcast I call Fail Corner. You already shared one example of a product that failed that you worked on. I'm curious if there's another, and the question is just what's the product you worked on that did not work out? Because people listening to this hear all these amazing successful people come on the podcast, share all these stories of success, endless success, but they don't hear the stories when things don't work out. And so this question is just, "What's a product you worked on that didn't work out and what did that teach you?"
turns.zh: 好的。我将带我们进入播客中我称之为“失败角”的重复片段。您已经分享了您开发的一款失败产品的示例。我很好奇是否还有另一个问题，问题是你开发的产品有哪些没有成功？因为听这个的人听到所有这些令人惊叹的成功人士来到播客，分享所有这些成功的故事，无尽的成功，但他们听不到事情不顺利时的故事。所以这个问题只是，“你开发过的一款产品没有成功，它教会了你什么？”

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: It's a very valuable point. My career has basically been a string of failed product on top of failed product. And I think that, "Yeah, the Google wave example's there." I worked for Hot Minute on Google+, which was another epic failure.
turns.zh: 这是非常有价值的一点。我的职业生涯基本上就是一系列失败产品的失败。我认为，“是的，Google Wave 的例子就在那里。”我在 Google+ 上的 Hot Minute 工作，这又是一次史诗般的失败。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Good one.
turns.zh: 好一个。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: I worked at this social networking startup called Secret, which burned hot for a bright minute and then blew up. And then there was an email startup that we did, and that was, again, very promising, and then that fizzled. So the co-founder of Canva and I worked on that one. So there's been a whole string of failures, but at each point, I think I learned something and I learned that I need to never make that class of failures or errors again. (01:15:01): And so Cash App was probably the big success for me that a product that I worked on that was very early on and grew to be this giant business and product that people love. So yeah, been my career is essentially taking the learnings from all these failures, getting some humility out of it in the process too, coming into things, willing to listen to other people's points of view, critical points of view, and not just thinking that I have all the answers, yeah.
turns.zh: 我曾在一家名为 Secret 的社交网络初创公司工作，该公司曾一度炙手可热，然后就爆炸了。然后我们创办了一家电子邮件初创公司，同样非常有前途，但后来却失败了。因此，我和 Canva 的联合创始人致力于这一项目。因此，出现了一连串的失败，但在每一次失败中，我想我都学到了一些东西，并且我知道我永远不会再犯这类失败或错误。 (01:15:01)：所以 Cash App 对我来说可能是一个巨大的成功，我很早就开发了一个产品，并逐渐发展成为人们喜爱的巨大业务和产品。所以，是的，我的职业生涯本质上就是从所有这些失败中吸取教训，在这个过程中也从中获得一些谦逊，进入事物，愿意倾听其他人的观点，批判性的观点，而不仅仅是认为我拥有所有的答案，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I bet all these products that failed had really beautiful code. A lot of really good architecture decisions were made. Some of them, some of them were awful in every way. So many reasons for it to fail. Incredible. Dhanji, is there anything else that you wanted to share or I don't know, double down on before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 我敢打赌，所有这些失败的产品都有非常漂亮的代码。做出了许多非常好的架构决策。其中有些人，有些人在各方面都很糟糕。导致它失败的原因有很多。极好的。 Dhanji，在我们开始激动人心的闪电回合之前，您还有什么想分享的或者我不知道的吗？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: I would say I think that we're in this era of a lot of change and people are scared or reticent or uncertain about where things are going. And I think that look at the things that matter to you. For us, it's open source, open protocols, improving access for everyone. I've been very lucky in my career to only work on products that are either free or almost free to anyone or they have a free tier and then you pay for some premium services and that are usable by everyone. So anyone can become a Square seller. (01:16:42): I remember even in the early days, people used it to pay each other as a peer-to-peer money transfer system and that's why we built Cash App and that was really successful on the back of that. So I think it's really look at the things that are important to you and optimize for them. It's not really that important that the technology trends are growing in a certain way because technology is here to serve us, and if we have an important reason for being and an important purpose, then we can make that technology serve us. And that's much more important than being deep with the technology or being at the forefront of every trend.
turns.zh: 我想说的是，我认为我们正处于一个充满变化的时代，人们对​​事情的发展感到害怕、沉默或不确定。我认为看看对你来说重要的事情。对我们来说，它是开源的、开放的协议，可以改善每个人的访问。在我的职业生涯中，我非常幸运，只开发对任何人免费或几乎免费的产品，或者它们有免费套餐，然后你需要支付一些每个人都可以使用的高级服务。所以任何人都可以成为 Square 卖家。 (01:16:42)：我记得即使在早期，人们也使用它作为点对点汇款系统来相互付款，这就是我们构建 Cash App 的原因，并且在此基础上取得了巨大的成功。所以我认为真正应该关注对你来说重要的事情并针对它们进行优化。技术趋势以某种方式增长并不那么重要，因为技术是为我们服务的，如果我们有重要的存在理由和重要目的，那么我们就可以让技术为我们服务。这比深入了解技术或走在每种趋势的最前沿更重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such great advice when there's so much to pay attention to and so much happening. So stressful to feel like I'm just not aware of all the things. I'm not as good as all these people I'm seeing on social media, but what's happening with AI, I'm just so behind. What I'm hearing from you is just like what is actually important to you? And just do that. Don't feel like you need to be the best at everything that's happening on top of all the latest AI news.
turns.zh: 当有如此多的事情需要关注、有如此多的事情发生时，这是一个很好的建议。压力很大，感觉我只是不知道所有的事情。我不如我在社交媒体上看到的所有这些人，但人工智能正在发生什么，我只是太落后了。我从你那里听到的就像对你来说真正重要的一样？就这么做吧。除了所有最新的人工智能新闻之外，不要觉得自己需要在所有发生的事情上都是最好的。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. And if it's not meaningful and fun, then you shouldn't be doing it probably.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。如果它没有意义和乐趣，那么你可能就不应该这样做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With that Dhanji, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 有了 Dhanji，我们就进入了非常激动人心的闪电回合。我有五个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Okay. Shoot.
turns.zh: 好的。射击。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see so many books behind you. So I love this first question. I'm excited to see what you pick. What are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 我看到你身后有很多书。所以我喜欢第一个问题。我很高兴看到你选择什么。您发现自己最向其他人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, so I very much of the opinion that you shouldn't read books that are about your daily work or your professional life. I read fiction, I read the classics, I read poetry, philosophy, history. These are the books I really enjoy. And I think it expands your mind and gives you creative ideas and helps you question things about the human condition. (01:18:39): And that's much more valuable than some self-help book or some get good at being an engineering manager book. So yeah, having said that, the Master in Margarita by Mikhail Bulgakov is one that I really love. It's a masterpiece of Russian literature. And then I've always been drawn to Tennyson's poetry and I find that in the times when I'm most uncertain or grieving, Tennyson's poetry has always resonated with me and helped me find a center.
turns.zh: 是的，所以我非常认为你不应该阅读有关你的日常工作或职业生活的书籍。我读小说、读经典、读诗歌、哲学、历史。这些是我真正喜欢的书。我认为它可以拓展你的思维，给你创造性的想法，并帮助你质疑有关人类状况的问题。 (01:18:39)：这比一些自助书籍或一些擅长成为工程经理的书更有价值。所以，是的，话虽如此，米哈伊尔·布尔加科夫的《玛格丽塔大师》是我真正喜欢的一部。这是俄罗斯文学的杰作。然后我一直被丁尼生的诗歌所吸引，我发现在我最不确定或最悲伤的时候，丁尼生的诗歌总是能引起我的共鸣并帮助我找到一个中心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Never heard these recommendations before. I'm really excited to check these out. Very cool for a CTO of a big tech company. What is a favorite recent movie or TV show you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 哇。以前从未听说过这些建议。我真的很高兴能检查这些。对于一家大型科技公司的首席技术官来说非常酷。您最近最喜欢的电影或电视节目是什么？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Alien Earth I think is pretty awesome. It's by Noah Hawley who did the Fargo TV series. And so it's someone with all of these incredible skills in high art filmmaking who's doing a pulp sci-fi show, and it just looks stunning and it feels stunning and it captures all of that essential alien pulpiness that makes it so interesting and fun. So I really like that, and I'm also watching Slow Horses, which I think is one of the better shows on TV.
turns.zh: 我觉得《异形地球》非常精彩。这是诺亚·霍利 (Noah Hawley) 创作的《冰血暴》电视剧。因此，一个在高艺术电影制作方面拥有所有这些令人难以置信的技能的人正在制作一部低俗科幻节目，它看起来令人惊叹，感觉令人惊叹，它捕捉到了所有重要的外星低俗内容，使其变得如此有趣和有趣。所以我真的很喜欢这个，而且我也在看《慢马》，我认为这是电视上最好的节目之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love Slow Horses. The new season's Out, think the fifth episode just dropped the day we're recording this. So I love that show. Alien Earth also just watched it, so creepy and just like all these slimy, gooey little creatures just crawling around.
turns.zh: 喜欢慢马。新一季已经出炉了，想想我们录制这个的那天第五集就已经结束了。所以我喜欢那个节目。外星地球也只是看着它，太令人毛骨悚然了，就像所有这些粘糊糊的小生物一样在周围爬行。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Yeah, I just love the aesthetic and they captured something essential about the original Alien and yeah, they do it, but every scene in Alien Earth feels like you're watching a painting or something or someone's reading a novel to you. It's really unfolds very thoughtfully.
turns.zh: 是的，我就是喜欢这种美学，他们捕捉到了原版《异形》中的一些基本要素，是的，他们做到了，但《异形地球》中的每个场景都感觉就像你正在看一幅画或其他东西，或者有人在给你读一本小说。它确实是经过深思熟虑地展开的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've never watched any alien content in my life and I really enjoyed Alien Earth. I will say the ending, I was just like, it felt like it kind of slowed down a bit. I'm just like, "All right, I guess I see where it's going now." But it was really fun to watch. Okay, next question. Do you have a favorite product you really enjoyed? Sorry, a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really enjoy? It could be an app, could be an gadget, could be some kitchen thing.
turns.zh: 我一生中从未看过任何外星内容，而且我真的很喜欢外星地球。我会说结局，我只是觉得，感觉有点慢下来了。我只是想，“好吧，我想我知道现在会发生什么了。”但观看起来真的很有趣。好的，下一个问题。您有真正喜欢的最喜欢的产品吗？抱歉，您最近发现了您真正喜欢的最喜欢的产品？它可以是一个应用程序，可以是一个小工具，也可以是厨房里的一些东西。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Well, I'm a gamer. I love playing games. So for me it's the Steam Deck, the Steam Deck OLED, which is their latest version. It's like this gorgeous piece of hardware that lets you play the best games out there, but it's totally extensible and customizable. And in this era where we're constantly told by big tech companies that we need to lock everything down, we need to lock down the user experience and customizability in order to have things work for people. (01:21:28): I think Valve showed that's totally unnecessary and totally wrong, and you can build the Steam Deck. You can install competing app stores, you can install Windows on it. You can treat it like a computer, write programs, which I have done to run on it. So yeah, I think it's an incredible thing and it looks beautiful and it works great. So yeah, big fan.
turns.zh: 嗯，我是一名游戏玩家。我喜欢玩游戏。所以对我来说，这是 Steam Deck，Steam Deck OLED，这是他们的最新版本。它就像这款华丽的硬件，可以让您玩最好的游戏，但它是完全可扩展和可定制的。在这个时代，大型科技公司不断告诉我们，我们需要锁定一切，我们需要锁定用户体验和可定制性，以便让事情为人们服务。 (01:21:28)：我认为 Valve 表明这是完全没有必要的，也是完全错误的，你可以构建 Steam Deck。你可以安装竞争的应用商店，你可以在上面安装Windows。你可以把它当作一台计算机，编写程序，我已经这样做了，可以在它上面运行。所以，是的，我认为这是一件令人难以置信的事情，它看起来很漂亮，而且效果很好。所以是的，大粉丝。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite life motto that you find yourself coming back to often in work or in life?
turns.zh: 您是否有最喜欢的人生格言，并且经常在工作或生活中提及？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: If you're not waking up in the morning feeling energized about what you're going to do that day in your professional life, then change something, quit if that's what it comes down to, or find a new way of doing what you're doing. Just don't accept what's meted out to you. So that's how I've tried to do things, and sometimes it works, sometimes not, but yeah, it's a good thing to ask yourself.
turns.zh: 如果你早上醒来时对自己在职业生涯中要做的事情没有感到精力充沛，那么就改变一些事情，如果确实如此的话就退出，或者找到一种新的方式来做你正在做的事情。只是不要接受给予你的东西。这就是我尝试做事的方式，有时有效，有时无效，但是，是的，问问自己是件好事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really love this advice. It's really hard to do that for a lot of people. Is there anything that has helped you get over that fear of just like, "Oh man, I'm going to quit this thing. I don't know where I'm going to go next."
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢这个建议。对于很多人来说，确实很难做到这一点。有没有什么可以帮助你克服那种恐惧，就像“天啊，我要放弃这件事了。我不知道下一步该去哪里。”

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: The main thing is telling yourself that a year from now, you're going to look back on what looks like a monumental problem, a life-changing thing, and you're going to be like, "Oh, that was so trivial." A lot of times we get into these traps where we're overthinking something or really nervous about making a change, but in hindsight, those don't seem that big. (01:23:05): And all the time that's passed since and all the events that have happened teach you that there's more to the world and it's never too late to do something useful or never too late to do something that's for yourself and improving yourself. So yeah, I think just kind of remembering that things are not as big or bleak or decisive as they seem in the moment is always important.
turns.zh: 最重要的是告诉自己，一年后，当你回顾这个看起来像一个巨大的问题、一个改变生活的事情时，你会说，“哦，那太微不足道了。”很多时候，我们会陷入这些陷阱，我们会过度思考某些事情，或者对做出改变感到非常紧张，但事后看来，这些似乎并没有那么大。 (01:23:05)：从那以后发生的所有时间和发生的所有事件都告诉你，世界上还有更多，做一些有用的事情永远不会太晚，或者做一些对自己有利并提高自己的事情永远不会太晚。所以，是的，我认为记住事情并不像此刻看起来那么大、黯淡或决定性总是很重要的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. So you were a mad scientist at Square for many years. Do you have another favorite mad scientist from pop culture or real life?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。所以你多年来一直是 Square 的一名疯狂科学家。您在流行文化或现实生活中还有另一位最喜欢的疯狂科学家吗？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: That's an interesting one. I think the image that always comes to my mind is Doc Brown from Back to the Future. I feel like he's the canonical mad scientist of my generation anyway, but there've been a lot in video games and stuff too, but he was the one that was like, "I'm just going to do this crazy thing because I almost have this burning desire, need to do it, and whether I want to or not, I must build this time machine." And he spends the entire movie trying to fix the problems that it creates. But yeah, he has always been a really fun character for me.
turns.zh: 这是一个有趣的事情。我认为我脑海中经常出现的形象是《回到未来》中的布朗博士。无论如何，我觉得他是我们这一代典型的疯狂科学家，但在电子游戏和其他东西中也有很多，但他是那种“我要做这件疯狂的事情，因为我几乎有这种强烈的欲望，需要这样做，无论我愿意与否，我都必须建造这台时间机器。”他花了整部电影试图解决它所造成的问题。但是，是的，他对我来说一直是一个非常有趣的角色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You know what? I think about Pinky from Pinky in the Brain.
turns.zh: 你知道吗？我想起《Pinky in the Brain》中的 Pinky。

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Oh yeah, that's a good one too. Yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，是的，这也是一件好事。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man. Dhanji, this was awesome. You were wonderful. Thank you so much for being here. Two final questions before we actually wrap up. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out, learn more about say Goose or anything else going on at Block? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 噢，伙计。丹吉，这太棒了。你太棒了。非常感谢您来到这里。在我们真正结束之前还有两个最后问题。如果人们想要联系、了解更多关于 Goose 或 Block 发生的其他事情，他们可以在哪里找到您？听众如何对你有用？

turns.speaker: Dhanji R. Prasanna
turns.en: Check out our GitHub pages for Goose and all of the other open source projects we have at Block. So there's a lot that's useful there. We do a lot on Android open source as well, so check that stuff out. You can always find me on LinkedIn, so feel free to connect. I'm very happy to be contacted. (01:25:06): And I would say the way people can be useful is, again, going back to this era we're in of a lot of change and uncertainty, I think people that demand more of their companies, of their employers, of their teams, demand something better. At Block, we always ask, "Can we default to making this open source? Can we build this for people that are not just us or our customers? Can everyone benefit?" (01:25:37): And I think that's particularly important in this era of AI where everyone's locking themselves in walled gardens and trying to capture parts of the platform that are emerging. So yeah, just demand more of people. The internet was created as a promise for open sharing of information to the benefit of all, and I think that AI should realize that for us. And so yeah, just demand that of people.
turns.zh: 查看 Goose 的 GitHub 页面以及 Block 上的所有其他开源项目。所以那里有很多有用的东西。我们也在 Android 开源方面做了很多工作，所以请查看这些内容。您随时可以在 LinkedIn 上找到我，因此请随时联系。我很高兴能与您联系。 (01:25:06)：我想说，人们的有用之道是，再次回到我们所处的这个充满变化和不确定性的时代，我认为人们对他们的公司、他们的雇主、他们的团队要求更多，要求更好的东西。在 Block，我们总是问：“我们可以默认将其开源吗？我们是否可以为我们或我们的客户之外的人构建这个？每个人都能受益吗？” (01:25:37)：我认为这在人工智能时代尤为重要，每个人都将自己锁在围墙花园中，并试图捕捉正在出现的平台的一部分。所以，是的，只是要求更多的人。互联网的创建是为了开放共享信息以造福所有人的承诺，我认为人工智能应该为我们实现这一点。所以，是的，只是要求人们这样做。

turns.en: A really beautiful way to end it. Dhanji, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 一个非常美丽的方式来结束它。丹吉，非常感谢你来到这里。

turns.en: Thank you, Lenny. I really appreciated it. Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，莱尼。我真的很感激。谢谢。

turns.en: I appreciate you.
